title: Sharing a train car with Tommy Ridgley
summary: Matassa and Ridgley rode the same car to New York despite segregation, with the train splitting in Florida and the Pullman porter staying silent.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But what the story is, which you even told me, Tommy told me the story, but you all got on the train, but you all slept in the same, it was the same compartment?
Oh, we joked about that, you know, because it wasn't legal in those days, you know. Black Iron One, and I think I was in the upper company.
You in the upper, Tommy was in the...

Yeah, and, in fact, we joked about it, because the train breaks into two trains, somewhere in Florida, you know, around Pensacola, somewhere like that, and part of it goes down the coast of Florida, and the other part goes up north. And, man, they're shunting these cars back and forth in the railroad yard about 2 o'clock in the morning. I said, man, that's a KKK separating this truck to this train. You know, what can you say?
But, yeah, I didn't give it a single thought.
I booked it, you know, in all the things.

Well, how did they... I wasn't defying anything. When you were getting on the car, don't they separate, then the Pullman, the Porter, or whatever, separate black and white? Well, yeah, luckily, the Pullman Porter kept his mouth shut.
You know, he could have said, I'm sorry, you know.

You ain't gonna sleep there, boy. But he was black, too. Right. And he just didn't say anything. He figured if nobody complained, you know. Yeah. Yeah. Mm. Wow. It was a lot wrong in those days. Oh, well, sure. Yeah.
